evidence_quotes.quote: The book provides a legal analysis of the right to water, combined with a qualitative case study which investigates and evaluates enjoyment of the right by people ‘on the ground’.

Chapter 5 continues the legal analysis but at a national and bilateral level and considers the provisions for a right to water under the bilateral agreements between Israel and the OPTs, commonly known as the Oslo Accords, and under applicable domestic law of Palestine and Israel.

The material presented is gathered from 45 semi-structured interviews which took place in the southern West Bank and which are based around questions related to the key elements of the right to water: availability, accessibility and safety;
The right to water in the Occupied Palestinian Territories (West Bank) Part III – A case study in the Southern West Bank 137

criterion_notes.c1: The Table of Contents and Introduction confirm that the book examines household and community drinking-water availability, sufficiency, accessibility, and safety in the southern West Bank.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: passes prima facie based on the Table of Contents and Introduction, as the book examines international human rights and humanitarian law, the Oslo Accords, Palestinian Water Law No 3/2002, Israeli Water Law 1959, Israeli case law, and Israeli Military Orders in relation to water access in the West Bank. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: unclear because Chapters 1–7 (pp. 8–196) are omitted from the retrieved publisher preview PDF; without Chapters 5 and 6, we cannot determine whether the empirical case study examines a concrete rule-type mechanism directly governing service access (such as military orders, permitting/connection rules, or regulatory allocation) versus general macro-conflict or doctrinal human-rights commentary.
criterion_notes.c3: The Introduction (p. 7) states that Chapter 6 reports a qualitative empirical case study based on 45 semi-structured interviews in the southern West Bank, indicating the full book is not purely doctrinal commentary; however, Chapter 6 (pp. 137–172, including 'Empirical study – design and methods') is completely missing from the retrieved PDF excerpt, preventing direct methodological assessment.
criterion_notes.c4: The Table of Contents (p. ix) and Introduction (p. 7) indicate that Chapter 6 analyses water availability (including a sufficiency analysis using WHO guidelines), access to water, and water quality, but because Chapter 6 is absent from the PDF, the actual empirical outcome reporting cannot be verified.
criterion_notes.c5: Only front matter, the 7-page Introduction (pp. 1–7), and References (pp. 197+) are present in the 41-page preview PDF; all substantive chapters (Chapters 1–7, pp. 8–196) and Appendices 1–2 are missing, so the full sample, unit of analysis, specific legal/administrative exposure in the empirical analysis, outcome measures, and study design cannot be verified from the accessible text (Criterion 8).

study_design: Qualitative socio-legal empirical case study (45 semi-structured interviews noted in Introduction; Chapter 6 methods text not accessible in preview PDF)
population_and_sample: Palestinians in surveyed communities in the southern West Bank (45 semi-structured interviews described in Introduction; full sample and unit of analysis in missing Chapter 6)
exposure: Human right to water legal framework, Oslo Accords, Palestinian and Israeli water laws, and Israeli Military Orders (Chapters 4–6 missing from preview PDF; specific empirical exposure not verifiable)
outcome: Water availability, sufficiency (WHO guidelines), accessibility, and water quality violations (Chapter 6 missing from preview PDF; empirical outcomes not verifiable)
rationale: reason: "full text not accessible". The retrieved 41-page PDF matches the record metadata (Cahill-Ripley 2011, Routledge monograph, eBook ISBN 978-0-203-82785-7), but it is an incomplete publisher preview containing only front matter, the Table of Contents, the 7-page Introduction (book pp. 1–7), and the References, omitting all substantive chapters (Chapters 1–7, book pp. 8–196) and Appendices 1–2. Although the Introduction and Table of Contents indicate that Chapter 5 covers domestic water statutes and Israeli Military Orders and Chapter 6 reports a primary qualitative empirical study of 45 semi-structured interviews on water availability and access in the southern West Bank, the absence of Chapters 5 and 6 prevents methodological assessment (Criterion 8) and prevents verifying the empirical population/unit of analysis, outcomes, and whether a rule-type legal/administrative mechanism directly governing service access is empirically analysed under either the narrow 2026-10-13 or plain Criterion 2 reading.
